title: Duke Wen of Teng, Part II

verses.t: Chen Dai said, "Your not going to see the feudal lords seems a small-minded thing. If you would now see them just once, at best you could make one of them a true king, and at the least a leading lord. Besides, the record says, 'Bend a foot to straighten eight feet.' It seems this could be done." Mencius said, "Once Duke Jing of Qi was out hunting and summoned his gamekeeper with a pennon. The gamekeeper did not come, and the duke was going to have him killed. [Confucius said,] 'A man of purpose does not forget that he may end in a ditch; a brave man does not forget that he may lose his head.' What did Confucius approve in him? That he would not go when summoned by a signal that was not his proper one. What then if I were to go without waiting for any summons at all? Moreover, this 'bend a foot to straighten eight feet' is spoken in terms of profit. If it is a question of profit, may one then bend eight feet to straighten one, if there is profit in it? Once Zhao Jianzi had Wang Liang drive the chariot for his favourite, Xi. In a whole day they did not get a single bird. Xi reported back, saying, 'He is the worst charioteer in the world.' Someone told Wang Liang of this. Wang Liang said, 'Let me try again.' He pressed until Xi agreed, and in one morning they got ten birds. Xi reported back, saying, 'He is the best charioteer in the world.' Jianzi said, 'I will have him drive for you regularly,' and told Wang Liang so. Wang Liang refused, saying, 'When I drove for him by the rules, galloping as one should, he did not get a single bird all day. When I cheated for him, cutting across the game, he got ten in one morning. The Ode says, "They do not miss the proper course of driving, and their arrows fly as though to split [the mark]." I am not used to driving for a small man. Let me decline.' Even a charioteer was ashamed to be partner to such an archer; even if by being his partner they could have taken game piled like hills, he would not do it. What would it be, then, if I bent the Way to follow those lords? And you are wrong besides: no one who has bent himself has ever been able to straighten others."

Jing Chun said, "Are not Gongsun Yan and Zhang Yi truly great men? When they are angry, the feudal lords tremble; when they are at rest, the whole world is quiet." Mencius said, "How can they be called great men? Have you not studied the rites? When a young man is capped, his father instructs him. When a girl is married, her mother instructs her; she sees her off at the gate and warns her, saying, 'When you go to your husband's home, you must be respectful and careful, and never disobey your husband.' To make compliance one's rule of right is the way of wives and concubines. To dwell in the wide house of the world, to stand in the correct place of the world, to walk the great Way of the world; when he gets his wish, to walk it together with the people, and when he does not, to walk his Way alone; to be one whom riches and honours cannot corrupt, whom poverty and low station cannot move, whom power and force cannot bend: this is what I call a great man."

Zhou Xiao asked, "Did the gentlemen of old take office?" Mencius said, "They did. The record says, 'If Confucius was three months without a ruler to serve, he was anxious and restless; when he crossed a border, he always carried his gift of introduction.' Gongming Yi said, 'Among the men of old, if one was three months without a ruler, others came to console him.'" "To console a man for being three months without a ruler: is that not too hasty?" Mencius said, "For a scholar to lose his position is like a feudal lord losing his state. The Rites says, 'The feudal lord ploughs [the sacred field] with the help [of the people] to supply the grain for the sacrificial vessels; his wife raises silkworms and reels the silk to make the robes. If the victims are not perfect, the grain not pure, and the robes not ready, he dare not sacrifice. And a scholar who has no land does not sacrifice either.' If the victims, the vessels and the robes are not ready and he dare not sacrifice, then he dare not hold a feast either. Is that not reason enough for consolation?" "Why did he always carry his gift of introduction when he crossed a border?" Mencius said, "Taking office is to a scholar what ploughing is to a farmer. Does a farmer leave his plough behind when he crosses a border?" Zhou Xiao said, "The state of Jin is also a state where men take office, yet I never heard that they were so anxious about it. If taking office is so urgent, why does the gentleman make such difficulty about it?" Mencius said, "When a boy is born, his parents wish for him a wife; when a girl is born, they wish for her a husband. Every parent feels this. But if, without waiting for the parents' command and the go-between's word, young people bore holes to peep at each other, or climb over walls to be together, their parents and everyone in the state will despise them. The men of old always wanted to take office, but they also hated to do it by an improper way. To go in by an improper way is of a kind with boring holes in walls."

Peng Geng asked, "To go about with dozens of carriages following you and several hundred attendants, living off one feudal lord after another: is that not excessive?" Mencius said, "If it is not according to the Way, one may not accept even a single basket of rice from another. If it is according to the Way, then Shun accepted the whole world from Yao and did not think it excessive. Do you think it excessive?" Peng Geng said, "No. But for a scholar to eat without doing any work is not right." Mencius said, "If you do not let people exchange the fruits of their work and trade their services, using surplus to supply what is lacking, then the farmer will have grain left over and the woman cloth left over. If you do let them exchange, then carpenters and carriage-makers can all get their food from you. Now here is a man who at home is filial and abroad is respectful to his elders, who guards the Way of the former kings to hand it on to later students, and yet he cannot get his food from you. Why do you honour carpenters and carriage-makers and slight those who practise benevolence and righteousness?" Peng Geng said, "The aim of the carpenter and carriage-maker is to get a living. When a gentleman practises the Way, is his aim also to get a living?" Mencius said, "Why bring in his aim? If he does work for you that deserves to be fed, then feed him. Besides, do you feed a man for his aim, or for his work?" "For his aim." Mencius said, "Here is a man who breaks your tiles and scrawls on your newly plastered walls, and his aim is to get a living. Will you feed him?" "No." "Then you do not feed a man for his aim, but for his work."

Wan Zhang asked, "Song is a small state. If it now sets out to practise kingly government and Qi and Chu hate it and attack it, what then?" Mencius said, "When Tang lived at Bo, his neighbour was Ge. The Earl of Ge was lawless and did not offer sacrifices. Tang sent someone to ask him, 'Why do you not sacrifice?' He said, 'I have nothing to supply the victims.' Tang sent him oxen and sheep. The Earl of Ge ate them and still did not sacrifice. Tang again sent someone to ask, 'Why do you not sacrifice?' He said, 'I have nothing to supply the grain.' Tang sent the people of Bo to plough for him, and the old and weak carried food to them. The Earl of Ge led out his people and waylaid those who had wine, food, millet and rice, and robbed them; those who would not give them up he killed. There was a boy bringing millet and meat, and they killed him and took it. The Book says, 'The Earl of Ge made an enemy of the food-bringers.' This is what it refers to. Because he had killed this boy, Tang made war on him, and everyone within the four seas said, 'It is not to enrich himself with the world; it is to avenge common men and women.' 'Tang began his campaigns with Ge.' He made eleven campaigns and had no rival in the world. When he marched east, the western tribes complained; when he marched south, the northern tribes complained, saying, 'Why does he leave us till last?' The people longed for him as in a great drought they long for rain. Those going to market did not stop, those weeding in the fields did not change their work. He punished the rulers and comforted the people, and it was like timely rain falling. The people were overjoyed. The Book says, 'We wait for our lord; when our lord comes there will be no more punishment.' [And again:] 'There were some who would not be subjects; he went east to campaign and gave peace to their men and women, who brought baskets of black and yellow silk, saying, "Let us serve our king of Zhou and be blessed," and became subjects of the great city of Zhou.' Their gentlemen filled baskets with black and yellow silk to welcome his gentlemen, and their common people brought baskets of rice and jugs of drink to welcome his common people. He saved the people from water and fire, and simply seized their oppressors. The Great Declaration says, 'Our martial might is raised; we invade their borders and seize the oppressors; our punishments are carried out, and it adds lustre to that of Tang.' [Song] simply does not practise kingly government, that is all. If it truly did, everyone within the four seas would lift their heads and look to it, wanting its ruler for their ruler. Great as Qi and Chu are, what would there be to fear?"

Mencius said to Dai Busheng, "Do you want your king to be good? I will tell you plainly. Suppose a great officer of Chu wanted his son to learn the speech of Qi. Would he have a man of Qi teach him, or a man of Chu?" "He would have a man of Qi teach him." Mencius said, "If one man of Qi teaches him while a crowd of Chu people chatter at him, then even if you beat him every day to make him speak like Qi, you will not succeed. But take him and set him down in the Zhuang and Yue quarters [of the Qi capital] for a few years, and then even if you beat him every day to make him speak like Chu, you will not succeed. You say that Xue Juzhou is a good scholar, and you have had him placed at the king's side. If all those at the king's side, old and young, high and low, were like Xue Juzhou, with whom could the king do wrong? If all those at the king's side, old and young, high and low, are unlike Xue Juzhou, with whom will the king do good? What can one Xue Juzhou alone do for the King of Song?"

Gongsun Chou asked, "What is the principle behind your not going to see the feudal lords?" Mencius said, "In ancient times, one who was not a minister did not go to see [the ruler]. Duangan Mu climbed over a wall to avoid [the Marquis of Wei]; Xie Liu shut his door and would not let [Duke Mu of Lu] in. Both of these went too far. If the ruler is pressing, one may see him. Yang Huo wanted Confucius to come and see him, but did not want to be thought lacking in courtesy. [By the rules,] when a great officer sends a gift to a scholar and the scholar is not at home to receive it, the scholar must go to the officer's gate to give thanks. So Yang Huo watched until Confucius was out and sent him a steamed piglet; Confucius likewise watched until Yang Huo was out and went to give thanks. At that time, since Yang Huo had made the first move, how could Confucius not go to see him? Zengzi said, 'Shrugging the shoulders and smiling to flatter is harder work than labouring in the vegetable plots in summer.' Zilu said, 'To talk with someone you do not agree with, and to see your face flush red as you do it: that is something I do not understand.' From this one can see what it is that the gentleman cultivates."

Dai Yingzhi said, "A tax of one-tenth, and doing away with duties at the border passes and in the markets: these we cannot do this year. Let us lighten them and wait until next year, and then stop them altogether. How would that be?" Mencius said, "Here is a man who steals one of his neighbour's chickens every day. Someone tells him, 'This is not the way of a gentleman.' He says, 'Let me cut it down: I will steal one chicken a month and wait until next year, and then stop altogether.' If you know it is not right, stop at once. Why wait until next year?"

Gongduzi said, "People outside all say that you are fond of arguing. May I ask why?" Mencius said, "How should I be fond of arguing? I cannot help it. The world has existed for a long time, with order and disorder in turn. In the time of Yao, the waters flowed backward and flooded the Middle Kingdom. Snakes and dragons lived in it and the people had nowhere to settle. In the low places they made nests [in the trees], and in the high places they made caves. The Book says, 'The overflowing waters were a warning to me.' The overflowing waters were the great flood. Yao had Yu bring it under control. Yu dug out the ground and led the water into the sea; he drove the snakes and dragons out into the marshes. The water then flowed in channels through the land: these are the Jiang, the Huai, the He and the Han. Once the dangers and obstacles were far removed and the birds and beasts that harmed men were gone, people could live on level ground. After Yao and Shun died, the Way of the sages declined. Tyrants arose one after another. They pulled down houses to make ponds, so that the people had nowhere to rest; they turned fields into parks, so that the people could not get food and clothing. Perverse teachings and violent deeds arose as well. With parks, ponds and marshes multiplying, the birds and beasts came back. By the time of Zhou [the last Shang king], the world was again in great disorder. The Duke of Zhou assisted King Wu. He put Zhou to death and attacked Yan; after three years he punished its ruler. He drove Feilian to the edge of the sea and killed him. He destroyed fifty states. He drove the tigers, leopards, rhinoceroses and elephants far away, and the world rejoiced. The Book says, 'Great and glorious were the plans of King Wen! Greatly were they carried on by the deeds of King Wu! They help and guide us who come after, all in rightness and without fault.' Then the age declined and the Way grew faint. Perverse teachings and violent deeds arose again. There were ministers who murdered their rulers and sons who murdered their fathers. Confucius was alarmed and made the Spring and Autumn Annals. The Spring and Autumn is the business of the Son of Heaven. That is why Confucius said, 'Those who understand me will do so through the Spring and Autumn; those who condemn me will do so through the Spring and Autumn.' No sage king has arisen; the feudal lords do as they please, and scholars without office talk wildly. The words of Yang Zhu and Mo Di fill the world. The talk of the world, if it does not go over to Yang, goes over to Mo. Yang's principle is 'each for himself', which does away with the ruler. Mo's principle is 'love for all alike', which does away with the father. To do away with father and ruler is to be a beast. Gongming Yi said, 'There is fat meat in your kitchens and there are fat horses in your stables, but the people look hungry and in the wilds lie those who have starved to death. This is leading beasts to devour men.' If the ways of Yang and Mo are not stopped, the Way of Confucius will not be made plain. Their perverse teachings deceive the people and choke off benevolence and righteousness. When benevolence and righteousness are choked off, beasts are led to devour men, and men will come to devour one another. I am alarmed by this. I defend the Way of the former sages, oppose Yang and Mo, and drive away wanton words, so that those with perverse teachings cannot rise up. What arises in the mind does harm to one's conduct; what arises in one's conduct does harm to government. Should a sage arise again, he would not change my words. In the past Yu checked the flood and the world was brought to order. The Duke of Zhou brought the barbarian tribes together under him and drove away the wild beasts, and the people had peace. Confucius completed the Spring and Autumn, and rebellious ministers and murderous sons were afraid. The Ode says, 'The Rong and Di he smote, Jing and Shu he punished, and none dared to stand against us.' Those who do away with father and ruler are the very ones the Duke of Zhou would smite. I too wish to set right men's hearts, put an end to perverse teachings, oppose crooked conduct and drive away wanton words, and so carry on the work of the three sages. How should I be fond of arguing? I cannot help it. Whoever can speak out against Yang and Mo is a follower of the sages."

Kuang Zhang said, "Is not Chen Zhongzi truly a man of integrity? When he lived at Wuling, he once went three days without eating, until his ears could not hear and his eyes could not see. There was a plum tree by the well, and grubs had eaten more than half of its fruit. He crawled over to it and ate one, and after three swallows his ears could hear and his eyes could see." Mencius said, "Among the scholars of Qi, I certainly count Zhongzi as the thumb [among the fingers]. Even so, how can he be called a man of integrity? To carry Zhongzi's standard all the way, one would have to be an earthworm. An earthworm above eats dry earth and below drinks from the Yellow Springs. The house Zhongzi lives in: was it built by [someone as pure as] Bo Yi, or was it built by [someone like] Robber Zhi? The grain he eats: was it planted by Bo Yi, or was it planted by Robber Zhi? That is something no one can know." Kuang Zhang said, "What does that matter? He makes sandals himself and his wife spins hemp, and they trade these for what they need." Mencius said, "Zhongzi comes from an old family of Qi. His elder brother Dai received an income of ten thousand zhong from his fief at Ge. Regarding his brother's income as unrighteous income, he would not eat from it; regarding his brother's house as an unrighteous house, he would not live in it. He kept away from his brother, left his mother, and lived at Wuling. One day when he came home, someone had sent his brother a live goose. Frowning, he said, 'What use is this cackling thing?' Another day his mother killed the goose and gave it to him to eat. His brother came in from outside and said, 'That is the meat of the cackling thing.' He went out and vomited it up. What his mother gave him he would not eat, but what his wife gave him he ate; his brother's house he would not live in, but at Wuling he lived. Is this carrying out his principle to its full extent? A man like Zhongzi could carry out his standard fully only after becoming an earthworm."
